title: Molecular Epidemiology, prenatal exposure and prevention of cancer.
ehr_evidence: The study did not use electronic health records; data sources were biospecimens (cord blood and maternal blood), personal air monitors measuring PAH exposure, maternal urinary PAH metabolites, and biomarker assays (DNA adducts, chromosomal aberrations, DNA methylation).
summary: A narrative review summarizing molecular epidemiology birth-cohort studies (NYC Mothers and Newborns Cohort and a Poland cohort) examining prenatal in utero exposure to air-pollutant PAHs and associated biomarkers of cancer risk.
key_findings: High prenatal PAH exposure was associated with a higher frequency of stable chromosomal aberrations in cord blood (FISH/whole-chromosome painting).
Maternal and cord white blood cells had equivalent PAH-DNA adduct levels despite an estimated fetal dose ~10 times lower than the mother.
Global DNA methylation levels in cord blood white blood cells decreased with increasing prenatal PAH exposure.
Global DNA methylation in cord blood was positively correlated with PAH-DNA adduct levels, suggesting adducts do not mediate the inverse association.
Methylation levels in cord blood did not vary significantly over time compared with blood collected at age 3.
Differential DNA methylation of specific genes (e.g., 5'-CpG island of ACSL3) was identified between low and high prenatal PAH exposure groups.
captured_features: Personal air monitor PAH exposure during pregnancy
PAH-DNA adducts in cord and maternal blood
Chromosomal aberrations in cord blood (FISH, whole-chromosome painting)
Global DNA methylation levels in cord blood white blood cells
study_design: Narrative review of birth cohort studies
population: Pregnant women and newborns/children in NYC (Mothers and Newborns Cohort) and Poland; prenatal/fetal exposure window
exposure_domain: Air pollution (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons) and environmental carcinogens, prenatal/in utero exposure
limitations: Measured overall/global DNA methylation rather than methylation status of specific genes.
Biomarker-based cross-sectional measurements with limited causal inference.
Relies on summary of prior cohort studies rather than a single primary analysis.
